title: Smooth muscle force is a balance

scenes.tts: Raise the pressure inside a garden hose, and it bulges. Raise the pressure inside a small artery, and the muscle in its wall pushes back. The artery narrows against the stretch. That answer is built into the muscle, not wired in from the brain. So what is the muscle sensing, and how does it make force?
scenes.visual: a hose bulges; a small artery narrows; the answer is built into the wall muscle, not the brain; what does it sense?
scenes.narration: Raise the pressure inside a garden hose, and it bulges. Raise the pressure inside a small artery, and the muscle in its wall pushes back. The artery narrows against the stretch. That answer is built into the muscle, not wired in from the brain. So what is the muscle sensing, and how does it make force?

scenes.tts: This muscle is smooth muscle. It has no troponin, so calcium cannot act on the thin filament. The switch sits on myosin instead. Calcium binds calmodulin, and calcium and calmodulin together activate myosin light-chain kinase. The kinase puts a phosphate on the regulatory light chain, and then the motor can cycle on actin.
scenes.visual: troponin crossed out; calcium to calmodulin to the kinase; a phosphate lands on the light chain; the myosin head strokes along actin
scenes.narration: This muscle is smooth muscle. It has no troponin, so calcium cannot act on the thin filament. The switch sits on myosin instead. Calcium binds calmodulin, and calcium and calmodulin together activate myosin light-chain kinase. The kinase puts a phosphate on the regulatory light chain, and then the motor can cycle on actin.

scenes.tts: But the kinase is only half the story. Myosin light-chain phosphatase takes the phosphate off, and it works the whole time. So force follows the balance of kinase and phosphatase. Calcium sets the kinase, so anything that changes the phosphatase changes force at the same calcium. That is calcium sensitization: more force at an unchanged calcium concentration.
scenes.visual: a seesaw: kinase alone tilts it, the phosphatase levels it; calcium tilts it one way; lowering the phosphatase tilts it further at the same calcium
scenes.narration: But the kinase is only half the story. Myosin light-chain phosphatase takes the phosphate off, and it works the whole time. So force follows the balance of kinase and phosphatase. scenes.tts: Now move the balance. Rho A activates Rho kinase, and Rho kinase inhibits the phosphatase. More phosphate stays on myosin, so force rises at the same calcium. The opposite arrow runs through nitric oxide, C G M P, and protein kinase G. In rabbit artery, the result is a lower calcium and, the authors read, an indirect activation of the phosphatase.
scenes.visual: Rho chain presses the phosphatase end up and force rises; the nitric oxide chain raises the phosphatase and force falls

scenes.tts: In mouse mesenteric arteries on a pressure myograph, calcium rose with pressure as normal. Arteries lacking G twelve and G thirteen in smooth muscle showed no active constriction and much less active Rho A. In control arteries, a Rho kinase inhibitor blocked the response. So this bed needs two things: a calcium rise, and Rho-dependent sensitization. How the pathways are wired upstream is unsettled.

scenes.tts: Flow in an idealized rigid arteriole is proportional to the pressure difference times the fourth power of the radius. Take made-up numbers: sixty millimetres of mercury and a radius of one hundred micrometres. Raise the difference to eighty millimetres of mercury, and a passive vessel stretched five percent carries sixty-two percent more flow. To hold flow constant, the radius must fall to ninety-three point one micrometres, a six point nine percent narrowing. Keep one rule: calcium sets the switch, and sensitivity sets the gain.
scenes.visual: an idealized arteriole ring and a flow-versus-radius curve from the equation; the dot moves from a stretched vessel to a narrower one
scenes.caption: Flow in an idealized rigid arteriole is proportional to the pressure difference times the fourth power of the radius. Take made-up numbers: 60 mmHg and a radius of 100 µm. Raise the difference to 80 mmHg, and a passive vessel stretched 5 percent carries 62 percent more flow. To hold flow constant, the radius must fall to 93.1 µm, a 6.9 percent narrowing. Keep one rule: calcium sets the switch, and sensitivity sets the gain.
